sources.news_title: Protests continue Saturday in Madison for man killed by police
sources.text:
Protests continue Saturday in Madison for man killed by police
Days after a police officer fatally shot a 38-year-old man, protests continue in Madison.
Since Corey Ruiz's death the afternoon of Wednesday, July 22, community members have gathered around the intersection of Williamson and South Baldwin streets, where Ruiz was shot. By Saturday, July 25, the pavement was filled with chalk writing, signs, flowers and candles. Tents, foldable chairs, fires, a portable toilet and a few mattresses were evidence of a days-long vigil.
Around noon July 25, a few dozen people marched through the area. Protestors engaged in chants and songs – including a rendition of "America the Beautiful" by the Raging Grannies of Madison. Several other community groups showed up, alongside neighbors and passersby. People took turns sharing their thoughts with a megaphone.
Ruiz was shot around 1:15 p.m. July 22 during an altercation with four police officers.
At news conference that evening, Madison Police Chief John Patterson said that the incident started when multiple officers attempted to arrest a man who was suspected of stealing bicycles and trying to enter unlocked vehicles. During the encounter with officers, the man drew a knife and injured an officer, who then fired their weapon, Patterson said.
Footage of the interaction captured by bystanders rapidly spread online, evoking criticism and calls for police reform. The video showed what appeared to be a white officer firing three shots at a Black man on the ground. Some government officials and policing experts have expressed concern with what they saw. Much of the conversation has also centered around the Madison Police Department's lack of body cameras.
Several Madison events have been canceled, postponed and had adjusted hours in response to the shooting and its community response.
The Madison Public Market postponed its grand opening, which had been scheduled for July 23. AtwoodFest, an annual neighborhood music festival, was canceled.
The Dane County Farmer's Market, which takes up the entire Capitol Square every Saturday April through November, from 6:15 a.m. to 1:15 p.m., closed early, at 10 a.m., in response to protests.
While little more than a dozen people were gathered around the Capitol building immediately following the farmer's market, the majority of protestors were concentrated at the Willimson and South Baldwin streets intersection – which has remained closed since the shooting.
Blockades consisting of cars, garbage cans, wood planks, traffic cones, mattresses, wooden pallets and furniture block off Williamson Street between the Willy Street Co-op and South Dickinson Street, and South Baldwin Street between East Wilson Street and Jenifer Street.
The City of Madison said in a July 24 news release that the closure will continue until further notice.
Ruiz's family retained prominent civil rights attorney Ben Crump to examine if police used excessive force in the shooting. The family spoke publicly alongside Crump at a July 24 news conference.
Contact Kelli Arseneau at (920) 213-3721 or karseneau@gannett.com. Follow her on X at @ArseneauKelli.

sources.news_title: Wisconsin’s capital city cancels signature summertime events after police shooting
sources.text:
MADISON, Wis. — In Wisconsin’s progressive capital city of Madison, where liberal residents have long embraced their history of political activism and protest, a police shooting this week has disrupted some of the largest and most popular summertime events and once again put the spotlight on persistent and deep racial divisions.
Corey Ruiz, who is identified as Black or Latino in Wisconsin court records, was shot and killed by a Madison police officer on Wednesday after a brief scuffle at the intersection of a city street just yards away from a popular 52-year-old food co-op in the heart of the city’s most liberal neighborhood.
It marks the third time since 2012 that Madison police have shot and killed someone in the same neighborhood. The shooting has sparked renewed calls for police reforms and forced the city that is 70% white to once again reckon with calls from the Black community to address racial justice issues.
Pressure from protesters, and sympathy for their cause, has also led to the cancellation or disruption of many of Madison’s signature summertime events.
“Our community has spoken loud and clear: this is NOT business as usual,” Black activist Clyde Mayberry posted on Facebook on Friday amid a string of cancellations. “Your decisions have helped ensure that this city continues to acknowledge the pain, the loss, and the call for accountability.”
Protesters took to the streets hours after the shooting, disrupting a popular Wisconsin Chamber Orchestra outdoor concert at the state Capitol that attracts about 30,000 every week in the summer. Protesters, many of whom were Black, stood over white concert attendees sitting at tables near the stage that cost as much as $1,800 to rent for the night.
Concert organizers canceled the event.
Threats of a protest on Thursday led the city to postpone the grand opening of a new public market, just a few blocks away from where the shooting occurred. A popular neighborhood festival near the shooting called AtwoodFest, scheduled to begin on Saturday, was also canceled in the face of potential protests.
“Our community and our Marquette neighbors witnessed another horrific officer-involved shooting just blocks from our festival grounds, leaving us in deep pain and justified anger,” organizers of the festival wrote. “In acknowledgment of what has happened far too often in our community and our country as a whole, this year’s AtwoodFest, themed ‘The Heartbeat of the Neighborhood,’ is canceled.”
And on Saturday, the popular downtown farmers market that attracts about 20,000 people each week around the Capitol building, was scheduled to shut down nearly four hours earlier than usual in solidarity with protesters.
“We mourn with our community,” market organizers posted on social media. “And we agree – business cannot proceed as usual.”
Investigations into the shooting continue. Civil rights attorney Ben Crump, who represents the Ruiz family, said on Friday at a new conference in the Capitol that the officer who fired the shots should face criminal charges.
Madison Police Chief John Patterson, who is white, has tried to calm tensions, even allowing protesters to overtake a news conference that he was leading along with the mayor inside the police department’s downtown headquarters on Thursday.
Patterson took questions from angry protesters, one of whom held a sign just feet away from the chief that said “corrupt cops deserve to die too.” After one protester hurled an insult at Patterson, the chief calmly responded, “I appreciate you being here.”

sources.news_title: Wisconsin officials open investigation into fatal police shooting
sources.text:
Authorities begin review of deadly encounter as community seeks answers and accountability
Wisconsin officials have launched an investigation into a fatal police shooting, as authorities work to determine the circumstances surrounding the incident. The investigation will examine the actions of the officers involved, the events leading up to the shooting, and whether established procedures were followed.
Officials have not released all details about the encounter whilst the review remains ongoing. Independent investigations into police shootings are typically conducted to ensure transparency and provide a thorough assessment of the facts.
Community members are calling for clarity, accountability, and a complete understanding of what occurred. Authorities have urged the public to allow investigators time to gather evidence, review available footage, and speak with witnesses.
The findings of the investigation will help determine the next steps and whether any additional action is required.

MADISON, Wis. (AP) — A police shooting in Wisconsin’s progressive capital city this week put the spotlight on persistent and deep racial divisions, prompting cancellations and other changes to popular summertime events as protesters said they were determined to continue public pressure for change in Madison.

Protesters took to the streets hours after the shooting, disrupting a popular Wisconsin Chamber Orchestra outdoor concert at the state Capitol that attracts about 30,000 every week in the summer.
The scene captures a familiar divide in Madison, a city that is more diverse than the state overall but still 70% white. Protesters, many of whom were Black, stood over white concert attendees sitting at tables near the stage that cost as much as $1,800 to rent for the night.
Concert organizers canceled the event.
Threats of a protest on Thursday led the city to postpone the grand opening of a new public market, just a few blocks away from where the shooting occurred. A popular neighborhood festival near the shooting called AtwoodFest, scheduled to begin on Saturday, was also canceled in the face of potential protests.
“Our community and our Marquette neighbors witnessed another horrific officer-involved shooting just blocks from our festival grounds, leaving us in deep pain and justified anger,” organizers of the festival wrote. “In acknowledgment of what has happened far too often in our community and our country as a whole, this year’s AtwoodFest, themed ‘The Heartbeat of the Neighborhood,’ is canceled.”
And on Saturday, the popular downtown farmers market that attracts about 20,000 people each week around the Capitol building, shut down nearly four hours earlier than usual in solidarity with protesters.
“We mourn with our community,” market organizers posted on social media. “And we agree - business cannot proceed as usual.”
A handful of protesters showed up at the Capitol as vendors were breaking down their booths at around 10 a.m.
“No one should be thinking this is just another Saturday,” said Reba Bergmann, who sat with Lilly Nimmer holding a sign that said “Justice for Corey.”
“It’s not life as normal,” Nimmer said. “We should be more mad. We should stand up for what we believe in.”
Charles Alt, 30, supported the decision to close down early.
“It’s important to keep focus on the real tragedy, which is that someone got killed,” said Alt, who was shopping at the market. “Missing some market time, that’s sad, but that’s not what’s important.”
But Rodney Hathaway, who was visiting Madison from Milwaukee, was caught off guard by the market’s early closure.
“It’s ridiculous,” he said. “This is peoples’ livelihoods. It’s just unfortunate. We have such a short summer season for these people to sell their wares.”
Investigations into the shooting continue. Civil rights attorney Ben Crump, who represents the Ruiz family, said on Friday at a new conference in the Capitol that the officer who fired the shots should face criminal charges.
Madison Police Chief John Patterson, who is white, has tried to calm tensions, even allowing protesters to overtake a news conference that he was leading along with the mayor inside the police department’s downtown headquarters on Thursday.
Patterson took questions from angry protesters, one of whom held a sign just feet away from the chief that said “corrupt cops deserve to die too.” After one protester hurled an insult at Patterson, the chief calmly responded, “I appreciate you being here.”
